extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, patent scholars, and inventors interested in patent allowance probabilities
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical measurement and interpretation of the probability that a U.S. patent application (progenitor) will be allowed, accounting for continuations, applicant type, technology field, pendency, and censoring. Uses USPTO internal prosecution-level data for cohort analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-action allowance rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of progenitor applications allowed without amendment at the first substantive examination (the "first action on the merits").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First action includes a search report listing relevant prior art that supports the examiner's decision. In the authors' data (1996–2005 cohorts examined to mid-2013) the first-action allowance rate was 11.4%. Trends in first-action allowance rate are used as an indicator of initial acceptance and changing examination scrutiny over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progenitor allowance rate ("allowance rate")
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of progenitor applications that are eventually allowed and patented without using any continuation procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progenitor allowance rate excludes outcomes achieved via continuation applications; in the paper's sample this rate was 55.8%. Progenitor applications are defined as applications unrelated to any previously filed U.S. patent applications. This metric measures the likelihood that an original filing (as filed) results in a patent without relying on continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family allowance rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of progenitor applications that produce at least one patent when allowance outcomes of continuation applications (serialized and non-serialized) are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family allowance rate counts any patent that issues in the family stemming from the progenitor. In the sample the family allowance rate was 71.2%. This metric captures the effect of continuation strategies on ultimate patenting success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation procedures — overall usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The fraction of progenitor applications that utilize at least one continuation procedure (serialized or non-serialized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study 31% of progenitor applications used at least one continuation. Measuring continuation usage is essential because continuations change how allowance rates should be computed and interpreted (e.g., progenitor vs family rates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-serialized continuations (RCEs) metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement of non-serialized continuation activity—primarily Requests for Continued Examination (RCEs)—which do not receive a new serial number and are docketed back to the same examiner (the progenitor is then considered abandoned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCEs are the most common non-serialized continuation: at least one RCE was filed by 19.5% of all applicants and 38.7% of applicants that received a non-final rejection. Including allowances of non-serialized continuations raises the allowance rate (authors note progenitor rate 55.8% -> 69.2% when including non-serialized continuations). Historical incarnations (CPAs, R129s, FWCs) are treated similarly; docketing rules changed in Nov 2009 (amended vs special new docket).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serialized continuations (CON, CIP, DIV) metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement of serialized continuation activity—continuation (CON), continuation-in-part (CIP), and divisional (DIV)—which receive new serial numbers and are treated as new applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serialized continuations may proceed in parallel with progenitor applications and can produce multiple patents from one progenitor. CIPs can contain new matter; priority date rules differ for new matter. As of June 30, 2013, 15.8% of progenitor applications resulted in at least one serialized continuation. Counting serialized continuations is necessary to compute family allowance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application abandonment rate / measurement of abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and measurement of abandonment events in prosecution (applicant does not respond by deadline or expressly requests abandonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment occurs at multiple stages (e.g., 2.3% abandoned prior to a first action decision; 14.5% abandoned between non-final and final rejection). Abandonment is a key component of allowance-rate dynamics because allowance rates are an 'opt-out' outcome influenced by applicants' willingness and resources to continue prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals after final rejection metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement of appeals to the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences (now PTAB) following final rejections and their allowance outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports 7.5% of final rejections were appealed and 41.4% of those appeals resulted in allowances. Appeals are an avenue by which final rejections can be reversed and thus affect progenitor and family allowance calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendency measures (first-action and disposal pendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing metrics: mean time from application date to first-action date, and mean time from application date to disposal date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mean first-action pendency was 21.1 months and mean disposal pendency was 29.1 months in the sample. Longer pendency correlates with higher abandonment and can bias observed allowance rates downwards for recent cohorts; pendency trends are used to explain temporal changes in allowance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censoring adjustment / maximum possible allowance-rate estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjusting allowance-rate estimates to account for censored (still-pending) applications by calculating upper-bound (maximum possible) rates if all pending applications and pending continuations were eventually allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors plot dotted/dashed lines representing the highest possible rates under the assumption all pending matters issue; they compute an upper-bound average family allowance rate of 72.3% (vs observed 71.2%). Using such adjustments justifies cohort cutoff choices (2005) to minimize censoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progenitor definition and sample selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule used to identify the unit of analysis: 'progenitor applications' are applications unrelated to any previously filed U.S. patent applications; sample restricted to utility patent applications filed 1996–2005 and examined through June 30, 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the progenitor as the unit allows linkage to continuations and accurate family constructions. The 2005 cohort cutoff minimizes censoring because average pendency is several years and few progenitors remained pending by mid-2013 (18,270, <1% of sample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant-type classification (large vs small; domestic vs foreign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorization of applications by applicant size and origin: small vs large entities (small = ≤500 employees qualifies for USPTO small-entity discount), and by first-named inventor address (U.S. vs foreign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification is used to compare allowance and continuation-use rates: large foreign inventors had the highest progenitor and family allowance rates (60.5% and 77%), small U.S. inventors had the lowest. Differences may reflect selection (which inventions are prosecuted in the U.S.) and resource constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-field aggregation (NBER patent-technology categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping USPTO technology classes into six broad NBER fields (Chemical; Drugs & Medical; Electrical & Electronics; Computers & Communications; Mechanical; Other) for aggregation and cross-field comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowance rates vary substantially by field (e.g., Drugs & Medical progenitor allowance 42.8% vs Electrical & Electronics 66.6%). Continuation usage patterns also vary by field (higher in sectors with lower progenitor allowance rates). Use of a standardized mapping (Hall-Jaffe-Trajtenberg) facilitates comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance-rate trends across cohort years
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracking how first-action, progenitor, and family allowance rates evolve across filing cohorts (year of application) to detect temporal changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study finds a substantial decline in allowance rates between 1996 and 2005 (e.g., cohort-average family allowance falling from ~70% for 1996 to ~40% for 2005 after accounting for censoring). Authors discuss plausible causes (2000 financial bust increasing abandonment; USPTO procedural changes increasing scrutiny; rising pendency) but do not claim definitive causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation with environmental covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Measuring contemporaneous correlations between allowance rates and macro/operational covariates such as percent change in real GDP, total pending applications, and total pendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A1 reports strong negative correlations between allowance rates and both total pending applications and total pendency (e.g., -0.925, -0.994 etc.) and a moderate positive correlation with percent change in GDP. These correlations are used to motivate hypotheses about drivers of allowance-rate fluctuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between allowance of claims and allowance of application as filed
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual criterion: allowance of some claims within an application after amendment is not the same as allowance of the original filed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because applicants amend claims during prosecution, counting only issued patents can obscure the extent of claim amendments and the scrutiny applied to the originally-filed claims. This distinction informs the choice among first-action, progenitor, and family allowance metrics when assessing examination rigor.
